paragraphs.heading: A crash that made the Moon
paragraphs.text: The giant-impact hypothesis, also known as the Theia Impact, is an astrogeology idea about where the Moon came from. It says the Proto-Earth was hit by a protoplanet about the size of Mars that shared Earth's orbit, probably arriving from the L₄ or L₅ Lagrange points. The crash took place roughly 4.5 billion years ago, early in the Hadean eon, when the Solar System was some 20 to 100 million years old. Part of the debris blasted out by the blow later gathered together again as the Moon. The impactor is sometimes called Theia, after the Greek Titan who was mother to Selene, goddess of the Moon.

paragraphs.heading: Clues that point to an impact
paragraphs.text: Several features of the Earth and Moon fit the idea. The Moon's orbit is lined up with Earth's spin, and both sit at a similar tilt to the ecliptic plane of the Solar System. Moon rock and Earth rock have identical stable isotope ratios, which implies they share an origin. The Earth–Moon pair also carries unusually high angular momentum: the motion stored in Earth's spin, the Moon's spin and the Moon's orbit adds up to far more than for the other rocky planets. A giant impact could have supplied that extra momentum.

paragraphs.heading: Heat, iron and missing volatiles
paragraphs.text: Moon samples show it was once molten to a substantial depth, though nobody knows how deep. Simply gathering a body of the Moon's size may not have released enough energy for that, while a huge collision could. The Moon also has a small iron core, so it is much less dense than Earth. Computer models suggest the impactor's core would plunge deep into Earth and merge with Earth's own core. The Moon would then form from lighter crust and mantle fragments flung past the Roche limit, leaving it short of metallic iron. It is also poor in volatile substances, which boil off at fairly low temperatures and could have escaped a violent event that the Moon's weaker gravity could not hold onto.

paragraphs.heading: From Darwin to Daly
paragraphs.text: In 1898 George Darwin proposed that Earth and the Moon had once been a single body. He thought a molten Moon had been flung off a spinning Earth by centrifugal forces, and this became the main academic view. Working with Newtonian mechanics, he calculated that the Moon used to orbit much closer and was slowly moving away. American and Soviet experiments with laser ranging targets left on the Moon later confirmed that drift. Still, Darwin's sums could not trace the Moon all the way back to Earth's surface. In 1946 Reginald Daly of Harvard changed the story, arguing that an impact, not centrifugal force, created the Moon.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea won
paragraphs.text: Daly's proposal was mostly ignored until a 1974 conference on satellites, where it was raised again and then discussed in Icarus in 1975. The astronomers Alastair Cameron and William Ward took a similar line, proposing a glancing blow on Earth by a Mars-sized body. Eighteen months before an October 1984 meeting on lunar origins, three lunar scientists told their colleagues to go back to their Apollo data and computers and come with something to say. At that meeting in Kona, Hawaii, the giant impact came out as the favorite. Before it there were backers of three traditional theories and a big indifferent middle; afterward there were essentially just the giant-impact camp and the agnostics.

paragraphs.heading: What is still unsettled
paragraphs.text: Signs of similar crashes have been seen in other star systems, where they leave debris discs. Giant collisions also fit the leading theory of how the Solar System formed. The energy of such a blow is expected to have melted Earth into a global magma ocean, and evidence of heavier material sinking into the mantle has been recorded. Even so, several questions remain about the best current models. No model yet follows the debris consistently from the impact all the way to a single moon.
